title: I'm deconstructing my faith
seoTitle: Deconstructing Your Faith: What to Let Go, What to Keep
description: Deconstructing your faith? A pastor who came to faith from atheism on what deserves to go, what is older underneath, and what to do this week.
summary: No panic and no shame: take your questions seriously, sort what you were handed, and dig for what is older.
askedAs: can you deconstruct and still be a Christian
what does the Bible say about deconstruction
answer: You're taking apart the faith you were handed, piece by piece, to see what will hold. Maybe it began with a leader who fell, a church that started to sound like a campaign, a purity talk you now hear differently, or an honest question that got a verse and a warning instead of an answer. Now everything seems to be coming down at once, and you're tired of two crowds, one afraid for you and one cheering you toward the door. Looking hard at what you were given isn't a sin, and some of it deserves to go. But sort as you go. The church culture you were raised in is not the same thing as the faith Christians have confessed for centuries, and you can lose the first without losing the second. You don't have to finish this tonight, and no one should rush you, but it's worth digging past the rubble to see what's underneath.
happening:
It usually starts with a single crack, and then one loose piece pulls on the next: *if they were wrong about that, what else were they wrong about?* Some cracks are loud: a scandal, a sermon you couldn't sit through. Others are quiet: a science class, a book, a prayer that went unanswered for years. Before long you're questioning everything, down to whether God is good and whether God is there.

It costs more than ideas. You may have lost friends who were your whole world, or you're afraid you will, and family dinners have grown careful. Old worship songs catch in your throat, and some verses come with the voice of whoever used them on you. Under it may run a fear you don't say out loud: *what if they were right, and I'm the one who's lost?* The people who stayed seem nervous around you, and the people who left seem to be waiting for you to finish leaving. If a church leader abused you, that is more than deconstruction, and [this page is for you first](/help/church-hurt).

You've probably heard one explanation at church: deconstruction is pride, or a wish to sin looking for permission. That's true of some people; a heart can decide first and shop for reasons afterward, and nobody is exempt, including the people saying it. But it can't account for the person who asked honest questions for years and was told to stop, or the one who believed so hard that the church's failures broke something. You don't test the weight of a thing you never leaned on.

The opposite explanation comes from friends who've left and much of the online world built around deconstruction: you're finally free. There's truth there too; some of what you were handed deserves to fall, and refusing to pretend is a kind of honesty. But this story shares a mistake with the panicked one. Both assume the package you were raised in is Christianity, so losing one means losing the other. And that world can have approved conclusions of its own, and less patience for anyone who comes out still believing.

Psychology adds a third explanation. Questioning the faith you grew up with is a common part of becoming an adult, and losing a community and its certainties at once can bring real grief, anxiety, and sleepless nights. If that heaviness has spread through your life, it deserves care of its own. Still, your questions aren't only symptoms, and they deserve real answers.

What all three leave out is a distinction, though you may have drawn it already. Taking apart a subculture is not the same as taking apart the faith. The subculture is the package: a political tribe, rules about dating and clothes, a style of worship, a habit of answering questions by forbidding them. The faith is older. Its oldest summaries say a great deal about a crucified and risen Jesus and nothing about a party or a dress code. You can take the first apart with a clear conscience. The second deserves its own hearing.

scripture.intro: Scripture knows about faith that was built badly, and about what's left when it comes down. These passages come from a singer far from God's house, a prophet who indicted the religious leaders of his day, an apostle writing to a church split into camps, and the day many of Jesus's followers walked away.

passages.text: My tears have been my food both day and night, while men ask me all day long, “Where is your God?” These things come to mind as I pour out my soul: how I walked with the multitude, leading the procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise. Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.
passages.reading: The heading names the sons of Korah, and the voice in this psalm once led the procession to the house of God. Now he is far from it, remembering God from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon (Psalm 42:6), while people keep asking where his God has gone. If you used to lead worship or a small group, or simply loved the songs and the people, this is your grief in the Bible's own words. The psalm takes its time with that grief. It argues with itself, its refrain coming back (Psalm 42:11; 43:5) because the hope hasn't caught up with the tears, and even the hope is in the future tense: "I will yet praise Him." It's a prayer for someone who can't sing the old songs today.

passages.text: This is what the LORD says: “Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths: ‘Where is the good way?’ Then walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it!’
passages.reading: Jeremiah began to prophesy under King Josiah (Jeremiah 1:2), and he had hard words for the religious leaders of his day: "They dress the wound of My people with very little care, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace at all" (Jeremiah 6:14). If you were handed easy answers for deep wounds, Jeremiah would recognize what happened to you. But notice where God sends people whose leaders failed them: back to the ancient paths, older than those leaders. The promise is rest, and Jesus later used the same words: "you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29). The people at that crossroads refused. You're standing at one now.

passages.text: By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds. For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work. If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward. If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.
passages.reading: Paul wrote this to a church in Corinth split into camps around favorite teachers, some saying "I follow Paul," and others "I follow Apollos" (1 Corinthians 3:4). His answer was that teachers are only builders. The foundation was laid once, and it is Jesus Christ. Everything else is material someone put on top, gold or straw, and on the Day Paul speaks of, the day of judgment, fire will test every builder's work. Notice whom the passage warns: the builders, teachers and pastors, and I'm one of them. Paul has that Day in view, not anyone's season of questions, but the line he draws holds now. Some of what you're watching burn may be straw that people like me built on the foundation and called gold. The fire tests the work. The foundation is Christ.

passages.text: From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him. So Jesus asked the Twelve, “Do you want to leave too?” Simon Peter replied, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.”
passages.reading: Jesus had just given a teaching so hard that his own disciples said, "This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?" (John 6:60). Many walked away, and the Gospel doesn't hide it. Jesus let them go without softening a word, then asked the Twelve if they wanted to leave too, and he let them answer. Peter answers with a question of his own, and he rests it on who Jesus is rather than on whether the teaching made sense. In the next breath Jesus told them one of the Twelve was a devil (John 6:70), and Peter stayed anyway, because it was Jesus he was following. Before you set Jesus down with everything else, ask Peter's question honestly.

whyHard:
Part of why this is so hard is the way many of us were handed the faith: as a package. Jesus came bundled with a church culture, a way of voting, rules about dating and clothes, and answers you weren't supposed to question. So when one piece fails, everything shakes. I'm a pastor, so I'm one of the people who hand the package over, and I can't pretend we always marked which pieces were essential and which were extras. Some of us preached the package as if it were the gospel.

Much of what's in that package deserves your critique. In *Soul Searching*, published in 2005, the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton reported on a national study of American teenagers and named the faith many of them had actually absorbed: moralistic therapeutic deism, in which God wants people to be good and nice, the goal of life is to feel good about yourself, and God stays out of the way until you have a problem to solve. There's no cross in it. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in *The Cost of Discipleship*, published in Nazi Germany in 1937, named another counterfeit: cheap grace, forgiveness without repentance, grace without following Jesus. Add a faith fused to a flag, and its mirror image, a faith fused to a cause, each sure that God is on its side; a purity culture that taught shame and called it holiness; churches that protected a leader's name instead of the people he hurt. Some of the sharpest critiques of all of it came from inside the church.

There's a danger on the other side too, and it deserves the same honesty. Taking apart is easier than building, and it can become a place to live. Some people spend years defining themselves by what they no longer believe. Others take apart a faith fused to one party and rebuild, almost without noticing, a faith fused to the other, with the same certainty and the same contempt for outsiders. A heart doesn't stay empty for long. If it isn't trusted to God, it will be trusted to a tribe, a cause, or a new crowd.

Scripture shows another way to take a faith apart. In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, workmen were repairing the temple when the high priest told the king's scribe, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!" (2 Kings 22:8). When the king heard it read, he tore his clothes, because "our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book" (2 Kings 22:13). Then he tore things down; at his command the objects made for Baal and Asherah were carried out of the temple itself and burned (2 Kings 23:4). And he recovered something: a Passover like none kept since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:22). He took apart what had been added by digging down to what was older. That's the difference between demolition and excavation. It isn't how much comes down. It's whether you're digging toward something.

What's underneath is smaller than the package, and older. When Paul summed up what he had passed on "as of first importance," it fit in a sentence: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Nicene Creed, first set down at Nicaea in 325 and expanded at Constantinople in 381, is still confessed in Orthodox, Catholic, and many Protestant churches, and it says nothing about a party, a dating rule, or a worship style. I came to faith from atheism, so I don't wave off the skeptic who calls this a retreat to the creed whenever the package fails. But the creed is centuries older than the package, and it asks you to believe more, not less: a virgin birth, a resurrection, a coming judgment. That's harder ground. Above it, faithful Christians disagree about a great deal, and you can take your time with those questions.

Some of what you're taking apart deserves to come down, and some of it was built by people like me. Let the straw burn. Just don't mistake it for the foundation, or mistake the people who failed you for the One they claimed to speak for. When the fire has finished with what we built, the claim at the center of the creed will still be there, a crucified man raised on the third day, and whether it's true is a question no one can answer for you, not your old church and not your new friends.

thisWeek.intro: Nothing here asks you to land anywhere this week. These steps are for sorting and digging, slowly and with company. Start with the first one tonight if you can, and let the others wait their turn.

steps.title: Sort the pile before you throw anything out
steps.body: Write down what you no longer believe or aren't sure of, one line each. Then mark each line by where it belongs: God and Jesus, the Bible, the church and its leaders, politics and culture, or the rules you were raised with. Don't argue with any of it yet. Just sort. If the list runs longer in some places than others, that shows you where the real work is.

steps.title: Read the Apostles' Creed, line by line
steps.body: Read [the Apostles' Creed](/resources/creeds/apostles-creed) slowly, with the notes. It grew out of the confession the early church taught new believers for their baptism. Mark each line *I believe this*, *I'm not sure*, or *I don't*. Then notice what isn't there: no party, no dating rules, no worship style, no timeline for the end of the world. The one ruler it names is Pontius Pilate, the governor under whom Jesus suffered. Whatever you decide, decide about this, not only about the package it came in.

steps.title: Do one thing Jesus said
steps.body: Read [the Sermon on the Mount](/study/bible/matthew/5) (Matthew 5 to 7) in one sitting, as if for the first time. Then choose one thing Jesus says to do and do it this week: pray for someone who has wronged you, give something away without telling anyone, or, before you worship, go and make peace with someone who has something against you. He ended that sermon with two builders, and the wise one hears his words "and acts on them" (Matthew 7:24). Some of what you're looking for is found by doing.

steps.title: Tell one person who won't panic or cheer
steps.body: Find one person you can tell the whole thing to: a pastor from outside your old church, a friend who believes and can bear your questions, or a counselor. Say it plainly: *I'm taking apart what I was taught, and I don't know yet what's left.* You don't need them to fix it or celebrate it, only to keep you company. And think twice before narrating it all online as it happens; an audience on either side can pull you toward its conclusions.

steps.title: Pray with borrowed words
steps.body: When your own words won't come, use older ones. Pray Psalm 42 aloud. Pray the Lord's Prayer once a day, slowly, and stop at the line you can't say yet. Jesus cried out the first line of Psalm 22 from the cross (Matthew 27:46), so borrowed words are no failure of faith. You aren't pretending to a certainty you don't have. You're letting words that held up other people hold you up for a while.

moreHelp.body:
What deconstruction needs first is time, honest reading, prayer, and good company, and a pastor who won't panic can walk with you through much of it. Sometimes, though, it travels with something heavier: depression, panic, fears about hell that won't let go, or the effects of real harm done in a church. Then it's time to add a doctor or a licensed counselor to the people walking with you. Questions of faith can arrive with a grieving, worn-out body, and both deserve care.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor you trust which counselors nearby are good. If you want a Christian counselor, look for one who can sit with your questions without pushing you out of the faith or hurrying you back in, and whoever you see, check that they're licensed in your state.

If you're afraid of someone at home, or someone uses God to control you, call the Domestic Violence Hotline listed at the end of this page to make a safety plan, and don't agree to couples counseling with someone who frightens you. If you're in danger right now, call 911. If you've had thoughts of not wanting to be alive, call or text 988 now, or go to the nearest emergency room.
signs: You've had thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now.
The heaviness has spread into your sleep, appetite, work, or closest relationships for two weeks or more.
Fear of hell, or of an unforgivable sin, keeps coming back however often you answer it.
Church buildings, worship songs, or certain verses set off panic, shaking, or dread.
A pastor or church leader abused you or someone else. Report any crime, and any harm to a child, to the police.
Someone at home threatens you, or uses God or Scripture to control or frighten you.
Your marriage or family has split into sides, and every talk about faith turns into a fight.
moreHelp.firstCall: A first call can be short. You might say, *I grew up in church, I'm questioning all of it, and it's wearing on my sleep and my family.* If harm in a church is part of it, say so. Then ask whether they're licensed in your state, whether they've worked with people questioning their faith or hurt in a church, and whether they'll take your questions and your faith seriously without steering you toward an answer. If the first counselor isn't a fit, try another.
moreHelp.cost: Help doesn't have to be expensive. Ask any counselor about a sliding scale based on income. Community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge less, many employers offer a few free sessions through an employee assistance program, and a church you trust may keep a benevolence fund. A pastor's time costs nothing.

helping.body:
If someone you love tells you they're deconstructing, your first job is to make sure they never regret telling you. If you're a parent, your fear makes sense. But fear talks too fast, and people stop confiding in someone who panics. Ask what, exactly, they're taking apart. It may be one church, a faith fused to politics, purity rules, or a leader who failed, and some of that deserves to come down. You may even need to admit that some of it came from you. Saying so plainly tells them they can be honest with you, too.

Keep loving them in ordinary ways: meals, texts, birthdays, the same seat at the table, and don't turn every visit into a debate. When many of his followers walked away, Jesus asked the Twelve, "Do you want to leave too?" (John 6:67), and he let them answer.

If you're a pastor, the person across from you may have taken the faith more seriously than you'd guess, and they're waiting to learn whether they can be honest and still belong. Own what the church got wrong, without defensiveness, and help them tell the straw from the foundation. That charge falls on me as much as on you.
say: Thank you for telling me. I'd rather know than guess.
What are you taking apart, exactly?
Some of what you were taught deserved to be questioned.
Nothing you decide will make me stop loving you.
Can we read something together, with no agenda?
dontSay: You just want permission to sin.
You were never really a Christian.
Deconstruction is pride, plain and simple.
helping.next: Pray for them without turning those prayers into hints. Offer to read the Apostles' Creed or a Gospel together, a little at a time, and let their questions stand. If you're a parent afraid your child is leaving, [What Do You Do When Your Child Leaves the Faith?](/life/the-wayward-child) was written for parents in your place. Keep the invitation to church open without making it the price of your company. If they say someone at home uses God to control or frighten them, ask how it's safe to reach them, and point them to the Hotline listed at the end of this page. If they mention not wanting to be alive, ask plainly, *Are you thinking about suicide?*, and stay with them while they call or text 988.

prayer:
God, I don't know how much of what I was taught was you. Some of it was fear, some of it was a flag or a cause, and some of it was somebody's opinion spoken in your name. I can't always tell the pieces apart, and I'm tired of one crowd telling me I'm lost and the other telling me I'm finally free.

If you're there, you know what I'm taking apart. Don't let me keep anything only because I'm afraid to lose it, or throw anything away only because someone hurt me with it. Whatever is older and truer under all of this, let me find it, and if you're the foundation, hold me up while I dig.

I remember when worship was easy, and I miss it. Some nights the only prayer I have is the one in the psalm: why have you forgotten me? Answer it in your time, and keep me honest until you do.

And if I'm about to walk away from you with everything else, ask me what you asked the Twelve, and give me the honesty to answer. Amen.

faq.a: Examining what you were taught isn't a sin; Scripture commends it. The Bereans "examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true" (Acts 17:11), and Paul told the Thessalonians not to treat prophecy with contempt but to "test all things. Hold fast to what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Jesus himself challenged traditions that set aside God's word: "You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men" (Mark 7:8). The letter to the Hebrews does warn against "a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12), but its picture is Israel in the wilderness, who saw God's works for forty years and hardened their hearts anyway, and its remedy is company: "exhort one another daily" (Hebrews 3:13). Honest asking is a different thing from a hardened heart.

faq.q: Can you deconstruct and still be a Christian?
faq.a: Yes, if what you're taking apart is a subculture rather than Christ. Paul put the center simply: "if you confess with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). A political tribe, a dating rule, and a worship style aren't in that sentence. But deconstruction doesn't always stop at the subculture, and some people find themselves doubting Jesus and the resurrection too. Doubt isn't the same as walking away: a father once told Jesus, "I do believe; help my unbelief" (Mark 9:24), and Jesus didn't turn him away. If that's your question now, [the page on doubt](/help/doubt) is for you. Either way, know which question you're asking: whether your church was right, or whether Jesus is who he said he was.

faq.q: What's the difference between deconstruction and reconstruction?
faq.a: Deconstruction takes apart; reconstruction builds again on what remains. When God sent Jeremiah to speak to nations and kingdoms, Judah among them, he gave him six verbs: "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). Four of them tear down, and that work was real, but it was never the whole commission. Reconstruction means digging until you reach what's older than the package, the faith of the creeds, centered on Jesus, and then building there slowly, in practice as well as thought. Rushing to swap old certainties for new ones only builds the same house in a different color.

faq.q: What if purity culture is part of why I'm deconstructing?
faq.a: Then some of what you're questioning deserved the questions. If you were taught to measure your worth by your purity, to hold girls responsible for what boys did with their eyes, or to expect a happy marriage as the reward for keeping the rules, you were taught a transaction, and it hurt people. You can grieve that without deciding the body doesn't matter to God. When some in Corinth treated the body as if it didn't matter, Paul told them what it is: "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:19). Shame calls you *damaged goods*, but no one is beyond the reach of grace.

It's a word some people use for themselves after leaving evangelicalism, a broad movement within Protestant Christianity. They leave for many reasons: its politics, its handling of abuse, its teaching on sex and gender, or questions nobody would let them ask. Where they end up varies. Some have left Christianity, some have found churches in older traditions, and some follow Jesus without a church for now. Leaving a movement isn't the same as leaving Christ, and you may find you've done one without the other.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. If he chooses, a few sentences in his own words, beside the paragraph that names the skeptic's suspicion of a retreat to the creed, on what he took apart on his way in and what he found underneath. Only as he tells it; the page stands without it. Two essays on the site (excavation-not-demolition, linked in the kit, and deconstruction-without-reconstruction, reached through the linked pathways) narrate first-person details of this (an atheism built at nineteen, years of demolition, a deconstructing reader at his table) that this page does not repeat; his slot can confirm or correct them.

Beside the sentences where the page says James is one of the people who hand the package over: if James wants to, something he once preached or assumed and later had to take apart, in his own words. The page makes no claim about his preaching.

As a father of five sons, what James would want a parent to hear when a child says they are deconstructing, in his own words and without describing his sons' faith. It would sit beside the paragraph for parents. (A drafted line at the end of whyHard about what he would want for his own sons was cut in review; if he wants a father's word there too, it belongs in his own words.)

The page leaves second-order questions open (it says faithful Christians disagree above the creedal floor). If James wishes, a sentence naming which questions he treats that way, and links to his own landings on the contested ones readers often bring to deconstruction (sexuality, women in church leadership, hell, the inerrancy debate), so a reader sorting the pile can find where he stands.

Checked: every passage and inline reference read in context with scripts/bsb.mjs --verses (Psalm 42:1-11 with 43:5; Jeremiah 1:1-3, 1:10, 6:13-16 with Matthew 11:28-30; 1 Corinthians 3:1-15, 6:12-20, 15:1-8; John 6:60-71; 2 Kings 22:3-13, 23:4, 23:21-25; Matthew 5:23-24, 5:44, 6:3-4, 7:24, 27:46 with Psalm 22:1; Acts 17:10-12; 1 Thessalonians 5:19-22; Mark 7:6-13 and 9:22-24; Hebrews 3:7-13; Romans 10:9). Smith and Denton now reads as reported in Soul Searching, published 2005 (the study itself was earlier), with the moralistic therapeutic deism summary brought closer to their own tenets; Bonhoeffer's cheap grace now names The Cost of Discipleship as published in Nazi Germany in 1937 (it had said writing in 1937); the Nicene Creed now reads first set down at Nicaea in 325 and expanded at Constantinople in 381, confessed in Orthodox, Catholic, and many (not all) Protestant churches; the Apostles' Creed now grew out of the confession the early church taught new believers for their baptism. Pilate is now the one ruler the Creed names, the governor under whom Jesus suffered (it had said the only politician). The step titled Read the oldest summary of the faith is now Read the Apostles' Creed, line by line (the page itself treats 1 Corinthians 15 as an older summary), and Borrow the oldest prayers is now Pray with borrowed words. Biography: the whyHard closing that spoke for James about his five sons was cut and replaced with an ending that leaves the resurrection question with the reader; the helping slot now notes it. Scripture: the 1 Corinthians 3 reading now says Paul has the day of judgment in view, not anyone's season of questions; the Hebrews 3:12 FAQ quotes the verse whole and reads it in its wilderness setting (hardening, with mutual exhortation as the remedy) instead of a trimmed phrase; Jeremiah 1:10 is set among nations and kingdoms; 1 Thessalonians 5:21 is set beside its line about prophecy; the purity-culture FAQ places 1 Corinthians 6:19 against the Corinthians who treated the body as if it did not matter; the psalm's own question (42:9) replaces a misattributed one in the prayer; Matthew 5:23-24 now reads make peace with someone who has something against you (not make things right with anyone, which could read as reconciling with someone who harmed you).
